title: a web cocoon is a place for becoming
content:
more on digital ecosystems and creative process

a website must be, first, a cocoon — before (and while) it becomes its own world. even after it’s existed for five or ten years, to keep a web world truly alive is to always embody its intention of ongoingness. a website as cocoon is: a semi-public internet vessel where you feel both safe and free to explore, dream, and process your ideas/creativity — in an ongoing way.

it’s in cocooning containers that we give ourselves permission to be soupy, incubative, and vulnerable. (and not a performative vulnerability with ulterior motives). there is a chaos, a tenderness, a spontaneity that comes with this space. you give yourself complete and total permission to be — and most crucially, to be seen.

a cocoon is nothing if not the tender membrane around process.

a web cocoon is, above all, an intention — rather than a specific shape, design, or output. it’s important that the container must support the intention. you cannot have a cocoon in a hostile environment, or in a carefully designed place where the system’s motives are not aligned with yours. that is to say: I’m skeptical of using social platforms as cocoons — even if your account is private and no one follows you. community is not the problem; the problem is that the system itself is designed to exploit your inner resources.

a web cocoon is for exactly for that — for nourishing your inner resources. maybe you’re wondering: why can’t I keep it all private, like a folder on my desktop, or a writing app, or a Notion database in the comfort of my computer? those are certainly creative cocoons — and I highly encourage an abundance of them. but they are not the same as web cocoons.

web cocoons, by nature of being on the internet, exist in a web — in relation to other real human souls. a folder in your desktop or a creative journal cannot trigger vulnerability in the same way that releasing oneself in the online world does. this vulnerability grapples with the question: how to be ourselves in relation to the world? this is a good place to grow.

part of this practice is about finding the right boundary between public and private. it’s about learning how to be yourself — in public — not to perform narratives of yourself, or scripted versions of yourself, or variations of yourself in order to be approved/loved/safe.

a web cocoon is about identity centered around process. the essence of a web cocoon is alive, soupy, messy — even after it is cultivated, structured, and deliberate. it pushes the boundaries. it makes you uncomfortable in a good way. when you decide you want to make a cocoon for yourself, and you decide to allow it to become a space for change. you give yourself permission to be always “in becoming” — and you decide that it’s okay to be seen that way.


-

*I first articulated these ideas around a digital cocoon while creating my recent iteration of house on the webs course.
author: Kening Zhu
